is a line break and a parenthesis). It can have white space and a line break at its ends, but it has to contain LaTeX, and
is text. A code span cannot be part of a formula, and a formula which is not closed before the end of the paragraph is text. A backslash which is itself escaped does not start a formula: in

block are not parsed as Markdown. The forms with dollar signs and the fenced
code blocks work as before, and the formula that starts first wins: in

inlineContent.text: The system’s HTML importer cannot typeset formulas, and it ignores the size of an image, so the HTML that the generator creates contains a placeholder for each formula. Once the importer has created the attributed string, the placeholders are replaced with
s. This is what the generator does for Mermaid diagrams as well (see
), and it works the same way:
draws the formulas, which takes some time, so the asynchronous methods (
) render them first. The synchronous method
cannot wait: it shows the formulas which have been rendered before, which
does ahead of time, and shows the others as code.
The images look like the text around them:
A formula within a line of text sits on the baseline of the text, so that the fraction bar is between the lines of the text, and a subscript hangs below it.

A formula has the colour of the text around it. This includes the colour of a link, and the colour of the light and dark variant of a generator. The renderer draws the formulas in black; the generator applies the colour of the text when it creates the attachment (macOS does not tint images by itself). The LaTeX commands
(the formula keeps the colour of its text) and
(it is not shown) are not reflected.
A formula is as large as the text, scaled with the font size of the text around it: formulas in headings are larger, and the rendering option
applies to them as well. Formulas are drawn for the font size of the generator, and the cache of the renderer depends on it.
A formula that is a block is a centered paragraph with at least
points above and below it. A formula that is wider than its line is scaled down to the width of the line, whenever the text is laid out, and
limits the width.
A formula that KaTeX does not understand is shown as code, a block with a note that has the message of KaTeX. The same holds for a formula that was not rendered in time (
The attachment of a formula has the attribute

, which holds the formula as it was written, for example to copy it as text, and an accessibility label with the LaTeX. The data of the attachment is a PNG image, so the formula survives copy and paste. RTF cannot contain images. RTFD export keeps them but loses the baseline offset of formulas within a line and sizes the images by the resolution of their files:
makes up for this, and
does it for you, see
renders formulas with
in a headless web view that is created when the first formula is rendered and released a minute after the last use (

). The web view cannot load anything from the network or from files: the style sheet and the fonts of KaTeX are part of its page. It draws up to a hundred formulas at a time, so a document with many formulas takes a fraction of a second; for each formula, it determines its size and the distance of its baseline from the lower edge. The images are PNG images at three pixels per point (
), which are black on a transparent background, and about 10 KB each. The renderer caches them: by default 2,000 formulas and 32 MB. A renderer of your own (
) lets you choose the limits;
is used if the generator is not given one. You can also call the renderer yourself if you need the image of a formula, see below.
Formulas in untrusted Markdown are as safe in the web view as in HTML: the options of KaTeX do not allow links and images, macros are limited, and formulas of more than 10,000 bytes are rejected (
); the page has a content security policy without network access. Use the limit
for the time a rendering may take.
